items.bodyEn: Hiroshige's Akasaka print looks into a hatago courtyard at dusk: a cycad in the garden, guests bathing and resting, serving women dressing by lamplight before supper. Akasaka's Ōhashiya, founded in 1649 and rebuilt after a fire around 1716, lodged travelers until March 2015; Toyokawa city now preserves it as one of the last Tōkaidō hatago still standing.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Fifty-three Stations (Hōeidō), Akasaka; Toyokawa city, Ōhashiya

items.bodyEn: The palm-like tree in Hiroshige's Akasaka courtyard is a 蘇鉄 (sotetsu, cycad): 蘇 'revive' plus 鉄 'iron'. Edo gardeners held that a sickly cycad recovered when iron nails were driven into its trunk or iron filings buried at its roots, so the plant was named for its cure. The belief is recorded in the 1712 encyclopedia Wakan Sansai Zue.
items.sourceNote: Wakan Sansai Zue (1712), 蘇鉄; Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, entry そてつ (蘇鉄)

items.bodyEn: In this station's 〜最中に the kanji are read さいちゅう: right in the middle of an action. Read さなか, the same word means the height of a season, as in the depth of winter. Read もなか, it is the wafer sweet filled with bean paste, named after 最中の月, the full mid-autumn moon that Edo confectioners shaped it to resemble.
items.ja: {食事|しょくじ}の{最中|さいちゅう}に
items.kana: しょくじのさいちゅうに
items.sourceNote: Daijisen, entries 最中 (さいちゅう・さなか・もなか)

items.bodyEn: Reduplicated gitaigo such as きらきら, のろのろ or どきどき are usually accented on the first mora when they work as adverbs: the pitch drops right after the first き in きらきら光る. Attach する and the same word commonly flattens to heiban, with no drop at all. The shift tells you whether the speaker is describing a manner or naming a state.
